passage:
Last year, when Anand and I were the two shortest boys in Class 4, I argued with him all through lunch. I told him our PT sir fell into the sandpit during long jump and came out covered head to toe. Anand said, "That never happened." I said, "I saw it!"
I really thought I had. I could see the sand in sir's moustache.
Then at home I watched my old cartoon, the one with the clumsy coach, and there it was: the coach falling into the sandpit, sand in his moustache. My face went hot.
The next day I told Anand, "You were right. It was the cartoon." He laughed and gave me half his samosa.
I'm Tarun, and I wasn't lying. My brain mixed up its drawers.

qa.q: Where did Tarun find the coach falling into the sandpit?
qa.a: In his old cartoon, the one with the clumsy coach.

qa.q: Why did Tarun insist, "I saw it!"?
qa.a: He could picture the sand in the moustache so clearly that it felt like a school memory; he had lost track that it came from the cartoon.

qa.q: What did Tarun do once he found the real source, and why was that a good choice?
qa.a: He told Anand the next day, "You were right. It was the cartoon," which cleared things up honestly after he had defended it so hard.

qa.q: How did Anand react to Tarun's admission, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: Anand laughed and shared half his samosa, which suggests he never thought Tarun was lying and was glad to move on. 😊

grounding: It shows a boy who sincerely defends a school memory that actually came from a cartoon, having lost track of its source.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 3, Wednesday
Madhav told his group today that a snake came into our classroom last week and hid in the cupboard, and that I caught it with a broom. He was very upset when the others said it wasn't true, and he went red defending it.
No snake came. I asked him gently, "Where do you think you saw it?" He paused and said there is a cartoon where a teacher catches a snake with a broom. Then, slowly: "Maybe that was the cartoon."
He wasn't lying; he believed it. I told the group so. Tomorrow we'll play a short game called "Seen, heard or watched?", where children sort things they remember.
Shankar

qa.q: Where did Madhav say the snake hid?
qa.a: He said it hid in the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Madhav go red defending the snake story?
qa.a: He believed it fully and felt hurt when others doubted him, because the cartoon memory felt like something from his own classroom.

qa.q: What game did Shankar plan, and how could it help?
qa.a: "Seen, heard or watched?", where children sort their memories, which trains them to notice where each memory came from.

qa.q: How might the group feel after Shankar says Madhav wasn't lying?
qa.a: They might stop teasing him and understand that mixing up a cartoon with real life can happen to anyone.

grounding: It shows a boy who sincerely defends a classroom memory that came from a cartoon, with the source lost.

passage:
Tuesday
I got into trouble today, and I don't think it's fair. At lunch I told everyone that Indu didi's school has a robot guard at the gate that scans your bag. They laughed. I said I saw it when Papa took me to drop her last month. I DID.
In the evening I asked Indu didi. She said there's no robot, only Ramesh uncle with a register. Then she said, "Little brother, that's from your robot cartoon."
I watched the cartoon again. There's a robot at a school gate scanning bags. Exactly the same.
Now I feel weird. I wasn't lying. I really thought I saw it. My head just stuck the cartoon on top of the real gate.
Tomorrow I'll tell them.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Who is really at the gate of Indu didi's school?
qa.a: Only Ramesh uncle with a register.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav feel it's unfair that the others laughed?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels hurt and misunderstood, because he sincerely believed he saw the robot guard, so being laughed at felt like being called a liar.

qa.q: What choice does Vaibhav make for tomorrow, and why is it brave?
qa.a: He decides to tell his friends it came from the cartoon, which is hard after defending it, but it keeps their trust.

qa.q: How might Indu didi see her brother's mix-up?
qa.a: She seems to see it as an honest mistake, pointing him to the cartoon instead of scolding him.

grounding: It shows a boy who mixes up a cartoon with a real school gate and sincerely defends it, not realising where the picture came from.

passage: In their village near Karad, Hrithik, eight, came home bursting with news for his older brother Tejas. "At school today, the headmaster's bicycle rolled down the slope, flew over the fence and landed in the pond with a big splash! Frogs jumped out!" Tejas laughed. "That's from the cartoon we watched last night, the one with the mouse on the bicycle." "No! It happened at school. I saw it." Hrithik's face went red and his eyes filled up. "Why don't you believe me?" Next morning Tejas asked the headmaster's son, Vikram, who said the bicycle had been parked by the office all day. Hrithik listened, confused. "But I remember the splash," he whispered. He wasn't lying. He just couldn't find where the splash had come from.

qa.q: Where had the headmaster's bicycle been all day, according to Vikram?
qa.a: Parked by the office all day.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's eyes fill up when Tejas laughed?
qa.a: He sincerely believed it happened at school, so being doubted felt unfair and hurtful 😢

qa.q: How could Tejas help Hrithik next time without making him feel called a liar?
qa.a: Tejas could gently ask where Hrithik first saw it, at school or in the cartoon, and say that everyone mixes up where things came from sometimes.

qa.q: What might Vikram have thought about the flying-bicycle story?
qa.a: Vikram probably found it funny and strange, knowing his father's bicycle never moved from the office.

grounding: A boy sincerely insists a cartoon scene happened at school, having lost track of where the memory came from.

passage: In a primary school in Valencia, Mateo, nine, told his classmate Layla at break, "Remember when Pip the hamster escaped last week and drove the toy car all the way down the corridor? Everyone screamed!" Layla stared. "That never happened. Pip was in the cage the whole time." "It did! I saw it!" Mateo turned to their teacher, Sofia. "Miss, tell her!" Sofia thought for a moment. "Mateo, I think I know that hamster. Wasn't it in the cartoon we watched on Friday, the one about the pet shop?" Mateo opened his mouth, then closed it. The toy car, the corridor, the screaming: all of it was the cartoon. "But it felt like our school," he said slowly. "It felt like Pip."

qa.q: Where was Pip the whole time, according to Layla?
qa.a: Pip was in the cage the whole time.

qa.q: Why did Mateo ask Sofia to back him up?
qa.a: He sincerely believed it happened at school and felt frustrated that Layla didn't believe him.

qa.q: How did Sofia help Mateo find the real source, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently suggested the cartoon they watched on Friday instead of calling him a liar, which let him check the memory himself.

qa.q: How might Layla feel when Mateo realises it was the cartoon?
qa.a: Layla might feel relieved to be right but also understanding, seeing that Mateo truly believed it.

passage: When I was eight, I told everyone that Manjula ma'am had brought a talking parrot to class and it said my name. I'm Abhinav, and I believed it with my whole heart. I described its green feathers and how it sat on her shoulder. My friends said it never happened. I got so angry I cried. Then Manjula ma'am herself said kindly that she had never owned a parrot. Years later, I found an old storybook at home: a teacher with a parrot on her shoulder that called out children's names. I had read it every night that year. Looking back, I wasn't lying. I just couldn't tell any more which pictures in my head came from the classroom and which came from the book.

qa.q: What colour were the parrot's feathers in Abhinav's memory?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav cry when friends said it never happened?
qa.a: Abhinav felt angry and hurt, because the parrot memory felt completely real and being doubted felt like being called a liar.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav understand the mix-up, and what could help children in the moment?
qa.a: Finding the old storybook; in the moment, a grown-up could calmly ask where the picture might have come from.

qa.q: How did Manjula ma'am respond?
qa.a: Manjula ma'am said kindly that she had never owned a parrot.

grounding: Shows a child sincerely mixing a storybook scene with a real teacher and defending it, not lying but losing the source.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Thursday.
During circle time, Sachin announced that a meteor had crashed into the school field during Tuesday's PT period, leaving a smoking hole. He described the flash and the heat on his face. Pradeep, sitting next to him, said, "That didn't happen. We played kho-kho." Sachin's face went red, and he insisted, close to tears. I remembered Sachin telling me on Monday about a cartoon where a meteor falls on a playground. I didn't say he was lying. I asked, "Is it possible the meteor came from your cartoon and the field came from PT?" He was quiet for a while, then said slowly, "Maybe they got stuck together." We walked out to the field at break. No hole. He laughed, a bit embarrassed, and relieved.

qa.q: What did the class actually play during PT on Tuesday?
qa.a: Kho-kho.

qa.q: Why did Sachin insist, close to tears?
qa.a: Sachin felt hurt and upset at being doubted, because the meteor memory felt real to him and he wasn't lying.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why was it respectful?
qa.a: The teacher suggested the cartoon and PT had got stuck together and walked out to check the field, without calling Sachin a liar.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt when Sachin insisted?
qa.a: Pradeep might have felt puzzled or annoyed, being sure they had only played kho-kho.

grounding: Shows a child sincerely mixing a cartoon meteor with a real PT class and defending it.

Thursday

Today at school I told Vaibhav that last week a boy in our class put a frog in the teacher's drawer and she screamed and fell off her chair.

Vaibhav said, "That never happened."

I said it DID. I remember the frog was green and slimy. But then Vaibhav said, "That's from the cartoon we watched at your house on Sunday."

In the kasba, Bhupen, nine, was telling the boys at the well about his classroom. "A goat walked right into class yesterday and ate Sir's register!"

His friend Kamal laughed. "No, it didn't. I was there."

"It did! It had a bell on its neck!"

"That's the cartoon on TV. The goat and the teacher. We watched it at the tea stall."

Bhupen opened his mouth, then closed it. He remembered the bell ringing. He remembered the register pages flying. But he couldn't remember which bench he'd been sitting on.

"I really thought it was our class," he said.

Kamal patted his shoulder. "You're not lying. You just mixed it up."

passage:
In Copenhagen, Anders, eight, came home from school and told his older brother Tariq, "Today a fire truck came to our school and the firefighters let us spray water!"

Tariq raised his eyebrows. "Really? I didn't hear about that."

"It happened! The water went on the roof!"

At dinner, their mother asked the school. No fire truck.

Anders frowned. "But I saw it."

Tariq thought for a moment. "We watched that fire truck show yesterday. The kids sprayed water on the roof."

Anders was quiet. "Oh." Then, "I wasn't lying."

"I know," said Tariq. "Your brain just mixed up the show and school."

qa.q: What did Anders say the firefighters let them do?
qa.a: Spray water.

qa.q: How did Anders feel when he said "I wasn't lying"?
qa.a: He felt worried about being seen as a liar and a little embarrassed, since he truly believed it.

qa.q: How might their mother feel after checking with the school?

passage: Omkar, you think you're the first to mix up the TV with real life? Listen to your Suraj ajoba. The school bus was about to leave on the last day before the Christmas holidays when Nilesh told his sister Sarika, breathless, "Today a boy in our class fell through the floor of the science lab, and the teacher pulled him out with a rope!"
Sarika stopped. "What? Is he okay?"
"Yes, he climbed out and his hair was all black and smoky."
At home Sarika phoned his class teacher, worried. The teacher laughed kindly. Nothing like that had happened. But in the Christmas party hour the class had watched a cartoon where a rabbit fell through a lab floor.
Nilesh turned red but insisted, "It was real. I remember it." He wasn't lying. He truly believed he had seen it in the lab.

qa.a: He remembers the scene vividly but has lost where it came from, so he feels sure, and embarrassed when told otherwise.

qa.q: How could Sarika talk to Nilesh about it without calling him a liar?
qa.a: She could say it sounds like the rabbit cartoon and gently ask whether he saw it on the screen or in the lab, treating it as a mix-up.
